subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Scientific Method and Investigation
subtitle: Fair tests, variables, evidence, data patterns, and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning
description: A source-faithful revision pack about how scientists ask testable questions, design fair investigations, collect reliable data, and explain results using evidence. It covers variables, observations, inferences, control groups, graphs, common misconceptions, and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning for middle school science.

data.targetWord: a planned way to answer a scientific question using observations, tests, data, and evidence

examples.en-US: A scientific investigation can test which fertilizer helps bean plants grow tallest.

data.targetWord: information gathered directly using senses or tools

examples.en-US: The plant is 18 cm tall is an observation.

data.targetWord: a logical explanation based on observations and prior knowledge

examples.en-US: Water droplets on a cold glass may lead to the inference that water vapor condensed.

data.targetWord: a question that can be answered using evidence from an investigation

examples.en-US: How does water temperature affect dissolving time is a testable question.

data.targetWord: a possible answer or explanation that can be tested with evidence

examples.en-US: If water is warmer, then sugar will dissolve faster is a hypothesis.

data.targetWord: a statement about what is expected to happen during an investigation

examples.en-US: Sugar will dissolve fastest in hot water is a prediction.

data.targetWord: any factor that can change in an investigation

examples.en-US: Temperature, time, and amount of water can all be variables.

data.targetWord: the variable the investigator changes on purpose

examples.en-US: Water temperature is the independent variable in a dissolving test.

data.targetWord: the variable the investigator measures or observes

examples.en-US: Dissolving time is the dependent variable in a sugar investigation.

data.targetWord: a factor kept the same so an investigation is fair

examples.en-US: The same amount of sugar is a controlled variable.

data.targetWord: a comparison group that does not receive the changed condition

examples.en-US: Plants with no fertilizer can be a control group.

data.targetWord: the group that receives the changed condition being tested

examples.en-US: Plants given fertilizer are the experimental group.

data.targetWord: the step-by-step plan for carrying out an investigation

examples.en-US: A procedure might list how to measure water, add sugar, and time dissolving.

data.targetWord: measurements or observations collected during an investigation

examples.en-US: Plant heights recorded over 10 days are data.

data.targetWord: data expressed with numbers, counts, or units

examples.en-US: 12 cm, 25 seconds, and 50 mL are quantitative data.

data.targetWord: descriptive data using words or categories

examples.en-US: Cloudy, blue-green, and strong smell are qualitative data.

data.targetWord: data or observations used to support or challenge a claim

examples.en-US: A plant growing 6 cm taller can be evidence for a light-growth claim.

data.targetWord: a statement that answers a scientific question

examples.en-US: More sunlight increased plant growth is a claim.

data.targetWord: the scientific explanation that connects evidence to a claim

examples.en-US: Reasoning explains why light helps plants grow through photosynthesis.

data.targetWord: one repeated test in an investigation

examples.en-US: Testing a paper towel three separate times means doing three trials.

data.targetWord: the ability to get similar results when an investigation is repeated

examples.en-US: Similar dissolving times across trials show repeatability.

data.targetWord: how trustworthy results are because methods are careful and evidence is repeated

examples.en-US: Multiple consistent trials make a result more reliable.

data.targetWord: how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value

examples.en-US: A thermometer reading close to the actual temperature is accurate.

data.targetWord: how close repeated measurements are to each other

examples.en-US: Mass readings of 10.1 g, 10.1 g, and 10.2 g are precise.

data.targetWord: a representation used to understand or explain something

examples.en-US: A water cycle diagram is a model.

data.targetWord: a group of interacting parts that work together

examples.en-US: A terrarium with soil, plants, water, air, and insects is a system.

data.targetWord: anything that has mass and takes up space

examples.en-US: Water, soil, air, and sugar are matter.

data.targetWord: the ability to cause change or do work

examples.en-US: Light energy helps plants grow.

data.targetWord: an investigation where only one main variable is changed at a time

examples.en-US: Changing only water temperature while keeping sugar amount the same creates a fair test.

data.targetWord: a preference or expectation that can affect how results are collected or interpreted

examples.en-US: Measuring one paper towel brand more carefully than another shows bias.

data.targetWord: a final explanation based on evidence from an investigation

examples.en-US: A conclusion explains which paper towel absorbed the most water and why the data support that result.

data.targetWord: a graph usually used to show how a measured value changes over time

examples.en-US: A line graph can show plant height each day.

data.targetWord: a graph usually used to compare categories

examples.en-US: A bar graph can compare average car distance on different surfaces.

data.targetWord: a pattern in data such as an increase, decrease, cycle, or no clear change

examples.en-US: A downward trend appears when dissolving time decreases as temperature increases.

data.targetWord: the number of samples or subjects tested in an investigation

examples.en-US: Using several plants in each light group gives a better sample size than using one plant.

data.targetWord: a conclusion that goes beyond what the evidence actually shows

examples.en-US: Saying tile always makes every vehicle fastest is an overclaim from one toy car test.

data.targetWord: a relationship or pattern between two things that does not automatically prove cause and effect

examples.en-US: Ice cream sales and sunburns may both rise in summer without one causing the other.

data.targetWord: an investigation used to compare design solutions using evidence

examples.en-US: Testing foam, gel, and air-cell padding can help engineers improve bike helmets.

In the sugar dissolving investigation, dissolving time was the ____ variable.

Repeated measurements close to each other are ____.
A personal preference that affects data collection or interpretation is ____.

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up ____.

data.title: Investigation Cycle
data.instruction: Put the common investigation cycle in order.
items: Ask a testable question.
Research or make careful observations.
Make a hypothesis.
Plan a fair test.
Collect data.
Analyze patterns.
Make a conclusion.
Ask new questions or revise the investigation.

data.title: From Data to Evidence
data.instruction: Order the steps that turn measurements into a scientific explanation.
items: Collect measurements or observations.
Organize the results in a data table.
Look for patterns in a graph or table.
Select data that answer the question.
Use the evidence to support or challenge a claim.
Write reasoning that explains the science behind the pattern.

data.title: Designing a Fair Sugar-Dissolving Test
data.instruction: Put the fair-test planning steps in a sensible order.
items: Choose water temperature as the independent variable.
Choose dissolving time as the dependent variable.
Keep water amount, sugar amount, cup type, and stirring speed the same.
Test cold, room-temperature, warm, and hot water.
Repeat each temperature condition for several trials.
Calculate average dissolving time and compare the pattern.

data.title: Writing a CER Explanation
data.instruction: Put the parts of a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning response in order.
items: State a claim that answers the investigation question.
Choose specific data that support or challenge the claim.
Include units and exact values when possible.
Explain the scientific idea that connects the evidence to the claim.
Avoid claiming more than the data show.
